content: Prenatal care refers to the medical attention and guidance provided to women before and during pregnancy. This care includes recommendations on proper nutrition, exercise, and vitamin supplementation, such as folic acid intake, which is essential for reducing the risk of neural tube defects. Routine prenatal care has significantly contributed to lowering rates of maternal mortality, miscarriages, birth defects, low birth weight, and other preventable infant health issues in developed countries. However, socioeconomic barriers often limit access to prenatal care in both developed and developing nations. Research in Canada and the United States has shown that rural communities and minority populations are less likely to have access to prenatal care, leading to higher rates of infant mortality and pregnancy complications. Prenatal care typically involves scheduled visits to healthcare providers. During the first two trimesters (weeks 1–28), these visits occur monthly. From weeks 28 to 36, visits are scheduled biweekly, and after week 36, they occur weekly until delivery, which usually happens between weeks 38 and 40. Physical Examinations Physical examinations during prenatal care include several key components: A detailed collection of the mother’s medical history. Recording the mother’s height and weight to assess overall health and weight gain during pregnancy. A pelvic examination to evaluate the reproductive organs. Blood and urine tests to screen for infections, anemia, gestational diabetes, and other conditions. Discussions with the healthcare provider to address any concerns or questions the mother may have. Ultrasound Obstetric ultrasounds are a common and safe diagnostic tool used during pregnancy, with over 35 years of established use. They are most frequently performed during the second trimester, around the 20th week of pregnancy. Ultrasounds serve several purposes, including: Confirming pregnancy (though this is less common). Detecting multiple fetuses. Determining the sex of the fetus. Identifying risks to the mother, such as miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, blighted ovum, or molar pregnancy. Detecting fetal malformations, such as spina bifida, cleft palate, clubfoot, or clenched fists. Monitoring the development of fetal organs, including the heart, brain, liver, stomach, skull, and bones. Evaluating the amniotic fluid and umbilical cord for potential issues. Ultrasounds are typically performed on a schedule or when abnormalities are suspected. Commonly recommended ultrasound timelines include: 7 weeks: To confirm pregnancy, rule out molar or ectopic pregnancy, and establish the due date. 13–14 weeks (in some regions): To assess the likelihood of Down syndrome. 18–20 weeks: For a comprehensive evaluation, including the detection of fetal anomalies and assessment of development. 34 weeks (in some regions): To evaluate fetal size and verify the position of the placenta.
